content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations regarding the use of home-based records (HBRs) for maternal, newborn, and child health. These recommendations are supported by a systematic review of studies, key informant interviews, and related documents. The findings highlight the characteristics and outcomes of various interventions involving HBRs, which are primarily paper-based or digital tools designed to improve health outcomes and communication between caregivers and healthcare providers. Key Findings from Included Studies: 1. Magwood et al. (2018): This study evaluated the effectiveness of parent-held child health records on maternal, newborn, and child health outcomes. The intervention improved parents' knowledge of child health and illness, enhanced communication between caregivers and healthcare providers, and increased healthcare utilization. The records were paper-based and multi-focused but lacked a health education component. 2. Dagvadorj et al. (2017): Conducted in Mongolia, this cluster-randomized controlled trial assessed the impact of the Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Handbook. The intervention reduced the risk of developmental delays in children and included a health education component. The handbook covered pregnancy, delivery, postpartum health, child growth, immunization, and dental health. 3. Elbourne et al.: This study focused on women holding their own obstetric case notes during pregnancy. The intervention improved women's sense of control and satisfaction with care. The records were single-focused and paper-based, with no health education component. 4. Lakhani et al.: This intervention provided caregivers with a home-based child health booklet. It improved caregivers' knowledge of child health and facilitated better communication with healthcare providers. The booklet was paper-based and multi-focused but lacked a health education component. 5. Lovell et al.: Women were given their maternity case notes to retain until delivery. The intervention improved antenatal care visits, exclusive breastfeeding rates, and maternal satisfaction. The records were single-focused and paper-based, with no health education component. 6. Moore et al.: This study provided a child health record supplement for children with disabilities. The intervention improved usability, communication between families and healthcare providers, and perceptions of care. The records were single-focused and paper-based, with no health education component. 7. Osaki et al. (2018): Conducted in Indonesia, this cluster-randomized trial evaluated the MCH Handbook. The intervention improved antenatal care visits, maternal immunization, professional delivery care, exclusive breastfeeding, and child health outcomes such as reduced stunting. The handbook was paper-based, multi-focused, and included a health education component. 8. Stille et al. (2001): This controlled trial in the USA used a graphic immunization card to improve vaccination rates. The intervention included an explanation of the card by providers and improved immunization series completion. The records were single-focused and paper-based, with a health education component. 9. Usman et al. (2009, 2011): These studies in Pakistan evaluated redesigned immunization cards and education sessions. The interventions improved vaccination initiation and completion rates. The records were single-focused, paper-based, and included a health education component. 10. Yanagisawa et al. (2015): This study in Cambodia assessed the MCH Handbook compared to standard health cards. The intervention improved maternal knowledge, antenatal care visits, skilled birth attendance, exclusive breastfeeding, and child immunization rates. The handbook was paper-based, multi-focused, and included a health education component. 11. Byczkowski et al. (2014): This study in the USA evaluated a web-based child health portal for parents of children with chronic conditions. The portal allowed access to laboratory results, medication information, and visit history. Parents reported concerns about usability and value. The records were single-focused and lacked a health education component. 12. Clendon & Dignam (2010): This study in New Zealand explored the societal role of child health record books (Plunket books) since their introduction in the 1920s. The records were paper-based, multi-focused, and included a health education component. 13. Grippo & Fracolli (2008): This study in Brazil evaluated a child health booklet covering child development and healthy care practices. The intervention improved family understanding and acceptance of the booklet. The records were paper-based, multi-focused, and included a health education component. 14. Hagiwara et al. (2013): Conducted in the occupied Palestinian territory, this study assessed the MCH Handbook. The intervention improved communication between caregivers and healthcare providers and maternal satisfaction. The records were paper-based, multi-focused, and included a health education component. 15. Hamilton & Wyver (2012): This study in Australia evaluated the Child Personal Health Record (CPHR) or Blue Book. The intervention improved parental engagement, knowledge, and communication with healthcare providers. The records were paper-based, multi-focused, and included a health education component. 16. Hunter et al. (2008): This study in the UK explored the use of adapted child health records for children in residential care. The intervention highlighted barriers to routine use and perceptions of care workers. The records were paper-based, multi-focused, and lacked a health education component. 17. Kelly et al. (2016): This study in the USA evaluated an electronic health record portal for hospitalized children. The intervention improved parental use and perceptions of the portal. The records were single-focused and included a health education component. 18. King et al. (2017): This study in Canada assessed an online portal for children in rehabilitation hospitals. The intervention improved access to records and communication with staff. The records were web-based, single-focused, and lacked a health education component. 19. Kitayama et al. (2014): This study in the USA explored desired characteristics of an online immunization record for underserved communities. The records were web-based, single-focused, and lacked a health education component. 20. Lee et al. (2016): This study in the USA evaluated the Patient Passport Program for hospitalized children. The intervention improved patient-provider communication and family satisfaction. The records were paper-based, single-focused, and lacked a health education component. 21. O’Connor et al. (2016): This study in the UK assessed the digital version of the Personal Child Health Record (eRed Book). The intervention improved documentation and communication between parents and health visitors. The records were web-based, single-focused, and lacked a health education component. Summary: The studies demonstrate that home-based records, whether paper-based or digital, can improve maternal, newborn, and child health outcomes by enhancing communication, knowledge, and care-seeking behaviors. Multi-focused records with health education components tend to have broader impacts, while single-focused records are often limited to specific outcomes such as immunization. The WHO emphasizes the importance of tailoring HBRs to the needs of the population and ensuring their usability and accessibility.
